qt: to the Commission Elena Kountoura (The Left) Subject:

Infertility is a serious and urgent public health problem1 that affects millions of citizens in the Union and is directly linked to the demographic crisis and the falling birth rates recorded in recent years. Despite this, access to infertility prevention, diagnosis and treatment, including assisted reproduction, remains uneven across Member States and is rarely supported by national health systems2. In view of the severe demographic crisis in Europe and the historically low fertility rate of 1.34 children per woman in the EU3, the high financial cost of treatments, which – combined with the rising cost of living, job insecurity and the imbalance between work and family life – acts as a disincentive for couples wishing to have children, and taking into account the global guideline issued by the WHO in November 2025 on the prevention, diagnosis and treatment of infertility4, can the Commission answer the following: 1.

Does it plan to propose a new European strategy for the prevention, diagnosis and treatment of infertility, in line with WHO recommendations, and to make the infertility challenge a priority of European public health and demographic policies?

Does it intend to support a specific funding mechanism in the new Multiannual Financial Framework to support the fertility and assisted reproduction sector in the Member States, as well as to reduce the financial and mental burden of fertility treatments on citizens?

The WHO defines infertility as a disease of the reproductive system and it is estimated that around one in six people of reproductive age worldwide experience infertility at some point in their lifetime. 2 Βλ. https://www.europarl.europa.eu/RegData/etudes/STUD/2023/757504/IPOL_STU(2023)757504_EN.pdf. 3 https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Fertility_statistics. 4 The guideline includes 40 recommendations covering the whole spectrum of prevention, diagnosis and treatment of infertility and advocates for their integration into the national health systems of all states (https://www.who.int/news/item/28-11-2025-who-issues-first-global-guideline-on-infertility). 1
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (16.10.2026) The Commission is not planning a European Strategy to tackle infertility, but is committed to supporting Member States through established frameworks and funding instruments. Member States are responsible for the definition of their health policy and for the organisation and delivery of health services and medical care1. Through the European Social Fund+ they can support access to infertility treatments for vulnerable persons, subject to national rules2, and use the European Regional Development Fund to invest in the necessary infrastructure and equipment. To complement Member States’ actions on sexual and reproductive health and rights (SRHR) for women, the Commission will carry out a mapping of practices in this area and develop a framework and methodology for systemic data collection on SRHR, as announced in the EU Gender Equality Strategy 2026-20303. Furthermore, the Commission will launch, in collaboration with the World Health Organization, a new initiative to monitor and analyse how to improve accessibility and quality of healthcare for women. Moreover, the EU4Health Programme has funded actions on sexually transmitted infections4, and on the safety, quality and efficacy of assisted reproduction therapies5, while Horizon Europe6 Cluster 1 ‘Health’7 may also fund collaborative projects on infertility. The Commission’s proposal for the new Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF) 2028-2034 prioritises investments in health and health research, under the European Competitiveness Fund. The ‘Health, Biotech, Agriculture and Bioeconomy’ policy window will continue to fund health-related projects. The MFF also provides that demographic change will be addressed as an objective of national and regional partnership plans.
